record.title: Students' Knowledge of Personalised Learning: How AI Can Help?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Personalised learning aims to align instruction with students' needs, interests, and motivation through responsive learning environments. However, many students demonstrate limited understanding of this concept, often associating it only with self‐paced learning or technology use. Such misconceptions weaken classroom implementation and may reduce student engagement and self‐regulation. This study aims to calibrate students' understanding of personalised learning and examine how artificial intelligence (AI) can be leveraged, directly and indirectly, to address key areas of misunderstanding and enhance effective implementation. The study involved 450 high school students aged 16–18 from selected schools in Kedah, Penang, and Perak, using a purposive sampling approach. Data were collected through a questionnaire administered during class after participants were briefed on the concept of personalised learning and the study purpose. Validity and reliability of the assessed constructs were evaluated using factor loadings ( λ ), average variance extracted (AVE), Cronbach's alpha ( α ), and composite reliability (CR), with acceptable thresholds of λ > 0.50, AVE > 0.50, α > 0.60, and CR > 0.60. Students' knowledge scores were analysed to identify aspects of personalised learning that were well understood and those requiring further clarification, providing an empirical basis for targeted instructional interventions. The findings indicate that the measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and validity. Students strongly associated personalised learning with needs‐based differentiation, particularly in project‐based and mixed‐ability contexts, but showed weaker understanding of learner autonomy, self‐paced learning, and digital facilitation. These results reveal a conceptual gap between theory and practice. Practical AI‐based strategies are proposed to enhance learning effectiveness and support adaptive, self‐regulated learning environments.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into mental health support settings, understanding how individuals engage with AI‐based tools for psychological support is increasingly important. This study introduces the nine‐item AI‐Assisted Psychological Support Use Scale (AAPSU), a behavioural measure of how people use conversational or generative AI for emotional regulation, self‐reflection, well‐being‐related decision‐making and support‐seeking. The scale development process included item generation, expert review, pilot testing, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and reliability testing. EFA identified two theoretically coherent subscales: self‐regulatory and reflective use (six items) and substitutive use (three items). CFA provided internal confirmation of this structure, with satisfactory model fit and strong factor loadings. Internal consistency was high for self‐regulatory and reflective use (Cronbach's α = 0.903), substitutive use (Cronbach's α = 0.888) and the total scale ( α = 0.919). Convergent‐validity analyses showed meaningful associations with attachment to AI systems, attitudes towards AI in mental health contexts and AI mindset. These findings support the AAPSU as a brief, reliable and theoretically grounded measure of AI‐assisted psychological support use while indicating the need for replication in more diverse samples.

record.abstract_text: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

record.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

record.title: Longitudinal association between AI dependence and pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition: the role of AI self-efficacy and perceived stress

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into teacher education has brought both opportunities and challenges. While AI tools are increasingly accessible to pre-service teachers, excessive dependence on AI may inadvertently undermine their critical thinking disposition—a key competency in professional development. Based on social cognitive theory, this study investigates the influence of AI dependence on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition, with a particular focus on the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and the moderating role of perceived stress. A three-phase longitudinal design was employed. The study tracked 461 pre-service teachers from Jiangxi Province, China. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the hypothesized relationships, including the mediation effect of AI self-efficacy and the first-stage moderating effect of perceived stress. Results showed that AI dependence significantly and negatively predicted pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition. AI self-efficacy partially mediated this negative association. Furthermore, perceived stress significantly moderated the first stage of the mediation process, such that the negative association between AI dependence and AI self-efficacy was stronger among pre-service teachers with higher levels of perceived stress. The conditional indirect effect was stronger at higher levels of perceived stress, and the index of moderated mediation was significant. The second-stage moderation was not significant. These findings highlight the potential risks associated with excessive AI dependence in teacher education: over-reliance on AI may undermine pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition partly through reduced AI self-efficacy. Moreover, perceived stress amplifies the negative indirect effect by moderating the first stage of the mediation process. This study extends social cognitive theory to the context of AI use and provides practical implications for promoting balanced AI engagement and critical thinking development in teacher training programs.

record.abstract_text: The increasing integration of AI tools in higher education has raised questions about how AI usage is associated with students’ academic behaviors. While AI can enhance efficiency, it may also be associated with greater academic procrastination. Existing studies have explored AI use and learning outcomes, but the psychological pathways underlying this association remain underexamined. Drawing on Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Moral Emotion Theory, this study examined the indirect roles of academic anxiety and self-control in the relationship between AI usage and academic procrastination, while also assessing whether AI guilt moderated these associations. In this cross-sectional survey, 782 students were recruited from two public universities in Guangxi, China, which were selected based on accessibility. Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were performed using PROCESS Models 4 and 7 in SPSS. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with academic procrastination. Academic anxiety and self-control both showed significant indirect associations, with completely standardized estimates of 0.129 and 0.119, respectively. Together, these indirect associations accounted for approximately 54.87% of the total association. In addition, AI guilt moderated the associations between AI usage and academic anxiety and self-control. Specifically, the positive association between AI usage and academic anxiety was weaker at higher levels of AI guilt, as was the negative association between AI usage and self-control. Within the scope of the variables examined, these findings provide context-specific evidence concerning selected emotional, behavioral, and moral-evaluative processes relevant to the associations among AI usage, academic anxiety, self-control, and academic procrastination among students at the participating universities.

record.title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for later life, with its benefits depending on how older adults appropriate, evaluate, and regulate its use rather than on technical capability alone. Existing research has focused primarily on technology acceptance, offering limited insight into how GenAI becomes valuable after adoption. Drawing on a socio-technical appropriation perspective, this study conducted a 14-day qualitative diary study with 16 community-dwelling older adults to examine everyday GenAI use. Thematic analysis identified four interconnected forms of appropriation: functional, creative, and relational appropriation, which co-created functional, experiential, and relational value; and critical appropriation, which regulated these forms of value while preserving human agency. We propose the GenAI Appropriation and Value Co-creation Framework (GAVC), explaining how older adults transform GenAI into a capability-expanding resource that supports later-life well-being. The framework advances appropriation theory and informs GenAI system design and literacy initiatives that foster active, productive aging.

record.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has challenged longstanding assumptions about the relationship between academic performance and student learning. When AI can generate essays, analyses, explanations and solutions, final products may no longer provide sufficient evidence that students engaged in the reasoning processes those products are intended to represent. This conceptual and theoretical paper proposes the IDEA framework as a thinking-centered approach to AI-enabled pedagogy. Drawing on scholarship in learning theory, reasoning, assessment and generative AI, the framework distinguishes among critical, systematic and creative thinking and connects these capacities to deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning. It further incorporates epistemic offloading and epistemic agency to examine how cognitive responsibility is distributed between learners and AI. The framework considers assignment structure, disciplinary context and learner development to determine when AI should be restricted, guided, or integrated. It also emphasizes making student reasoning, judgment, reflection and intellectual ownership visible. By shifting the focus from regulating AI use to identifying the cognitive and epistemic work that must remain meaningfully with the learner, IDEA provides a concept-to-application model for aligning generative AI with the purposes of teaching, assessment and curriculum in higher education.

record.title: Machine learning-based Taylor cone analysis for electrospinning process-window identification and cell-laden nanofiber scaffold fabrication

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Electrospinning is a powerful biofabrication technique for constructing fibrous scaffolds that mimic extracellular matrix architectures. However, the process is highly nonlinear and involves strongly coupled parameters, making fiber architecture and biological performance difficult to control empirically and limits reproducibility. Most ML studies still focus on static correlations between processing parameters and outcomes rather than on dynamic modeling of electrospinning evolution and regulation, thereby hindering real-time, precise process control. Here, we establish a data-driven framework that links process parameters, Taylor cone geometry, and nanofiber/cell outcomes through high-speed imaging and ML. A custom image-processing pipeline is developed to automatically extract cone angle, height, and width from in situ images with improved accuracy via a rotating-ray–based geometric algorithm. Using datasets collected from three representative polymer systems PVDF, PVB, and PEO, RF models outperform SVM and MDL, achieving moderate-to-good prediction of Taylor cone descriptors ( R 2 ≈ 0.57-0.83) across varied voltages, flow rates, and needle–collector distances. We further extend this framework to PEO-based cell electrospinning. By correlating predicted cone geometries with experimentally measured viability of 293 T cells and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells, we identify a Taylor cone ‘safe window’ that simultaneously stabilizes jet formation and preserves cell survival (>95%). Guided by this window, a bilayer cell-laden scaffold comprising a PVB support layer and a PEO–cell layer is fabricated with improved process robustness. This enables stable delivery of high-density, highly viable cells and facilitates the fabrication of three-dimensional cell-laden nanofiber scaffolds. Overall, this ML-guided Taylor cone analysis strategy provides a quantitative framework for process-window identification in polymer and cell electrospinning, and may support future integration with real-time monitoring, online inference, and closed-loop control in intelligent biofabrication.

record.title: Does Generative AI Enhance or Erode Critical Thinking in Music Education?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Critical thinking has been a cornerstone of education. Some wonder what these technological advancements will do to people’s thinking and, more specifically, to critical thinking. In this chapter, we look at some of the potential affordances and limitations to critical thinking regarding artificial intelligence (AI) and how educators might respond. We address three aspects of critical thinking as outlined by research. First, critical thinking is the capacity to problem-solve. AI has the potential to help solve problems, although it might also erode one’s abilities, what some researchers call “cognitive offloading.” Second, critical thinking is a social process where people come together to think and challenge ideas. AI and newer technologies in general might bring people together; however, they might lead to what we are calling social offloading. Third, critical thinking is dependent on a diversity of ideas. Generative AI has the potential to synthesize a diversity of information and provide greater access; however, its models and algorithms may slowly limit this diversity. We situate these conceptions of critical thinking in concert with AI and provide pedagogical considerations for music educators to move toward a more process-based approach to critical thinking. This includes creating purposeful moments for students to work collaboratively—or to gather—and think critically, while also using AI tools.

record.abstract_text: Abstract The National Weather Service (NWS) recently developed an AI-powered neural machine translation system to deliver potentially life-saving weather warnings to the 68.8 million Americans who speak a language other than English at home. This forum piece makes the case that applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have a vital and largely untapped role in the continued development of this technology. First, dialect and register variation across multilingual groups demands ongoing sociolinguistic attention, as translation differences affect how people understand and conceptualize risk. Second, the metrics NWS uses to evaluate translation quality leave communicative effectiveness unmeasured, and demographic categories used to identify target audiences miss the breadth of bilingual experience, both of which applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have the tools to address. Third, indigenous, oral-tradition, and signed languages present challenges that corpus-based training cannot resolve alone, and reaching these groups will take community linguistic fieldwork and delivery beyond text. Warnings are only as effective as their comprehension, and applied linguistics can increase understanding and action during extreme weather events across a multilingual nation.

record.title: The boundaries of copyright law in regulating AI-generated content: lessons from the UK

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Journal of Intellectual Property Law & Practice
record.abstract_text: Abstract Section 9(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 attributes authorship of a computer-generated work to the person who undertakes the arrangements necessary for its creation. The rapid development of generative AI has renewed attention to this provision, yet its legal function remains uncertain. In particular, its relationship with the originality requirement is unresolved, and it is unclear whether section 9(3) should be understood as an authorship rule or as a mechanism for protecting investment in authorless outputs. This article reassesses section 9(3) through doctrinal and comparative analysis. It argues that AI-assisted works involving sufficient human creative contribution can be accommodated within the existing framework of human authorship and originality. Comparative experience from China and the United States supports this conclusion. The potential independent role of section 9(3) should therefore be confined to the genuinely authorless AI-generated outputs. Protection of such outputs, however, cannot be justified merely because copyright is unavailable. The article argues that the future of section 9(3) should depend on whether it continues to serve a distinct and defensible social or economic function. Until the legal position is clarified or changed, courts should first apply general copyright principles and avoid assuming that section 9(3) automatically displaces the originality requirement. If special protection for authorless outputs is retained in the future, its scope and duration should be designed in accordance with the specific policy objectives that such protection is intended to serve.

record.abstract_text: Purpose Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction. Findings AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy. Originality/value This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

record.abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is to develop an understanding of AI influencer transparency and its effects on affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. record.abstract_text: Abstract The application of artificial intelligence technology in education is becoming increasingly widespread, but there is no consensus yet on its impact on learners’ critical thinking. record.abstract_text: Abstract Predicting whether a pull request (PR) will be merged, rejected, or left unre solved is a recurring problem in empirical software engineering, yet it remains unclear how much explicit fusion of code changes and reviewer comments adds over simpler designs, and conclusions drawn from a single training run can be misleading. A CodeBERT–RoBERTa hybrid with bidirectional cross-modal attention is compared with concatenation and late-fusion variants, four alternative code encoders (GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, CodeReviewer), unimodal baselines, and two re-implemented prior systems, using five random seeds per model. Review comments alone are about as informative as code alone, and combining them adds roughly 1.6–1.9 pp. Project identity is strongly associated with the outcome (Cram´er’s V = 0.60), so the random split used here probably overstates generalisation. record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Home-based exercise programs for congenital muscular torticollis (CMT) depend heavily on caregivers, yet adherence is often hindered by cognitive and emotional burdens. Objective This study conducted a formative usability evaluation of an AI-based CMT rehabilitation system comprising a clinician web interface and a caregiver mobile app to identify usability-related issues and preliminary design requirements during early development. Methods A formative usability evaluation was conducted with 8 clinical experts (rehabilitation physicians, nurses, and physical therapists). Participants engaged in focus group interviews (FGIs) following a demonstration of the system and completed the System Usability Scale (SUS) for the overall system, including a proxy evaluation of the caregiver mobile app. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis, and SUS scores were analyzed descriptively as a supplementary quantitative measure of perceived usability. Results The thematic analysis identified 2 core themes, “Usability Barriers of the CMT Rehabilitation System” and “Improvement Requirements,” encompassing 10 subthemes and 21 concepts. Key findings highlighted concerns regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback and the need to simplify data visualization to reduce the potential cognitive burden on caregivers. The mean SUS score for the overall system was 73.44 (SD 18.01). This result was interpreted descriptively and considered supplementary to the qualitative findings. Conclusions The formative evaluation identified preliminary usability strengths and areas for improvement from clinicians’ perspectives, with particular concerns regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback. The experts emphasized that the AI-based CMT rehabilitation system should function as a therapeutic bridge between clinicians and caregivers. As actual caregivers were not included in this evaluation, the findings represent preliminary formative design inputs based on clinicians’ proxy perspectives rather than evidence of usability for caregivers. Future iterations should incorporate the identified improvements and undergo evaluation with actual caregivers in home environments, along with separate technical verification of the accuracy of the AI feedback algorithm.

record.abstract_text: Unlabelled: Clinical AI is moving from systems that generate discrete predictions and recommendations toward agents capable of pursuing clinical objectives through repeated tool use, communication, planning, and state-changing actions. Emerging systems support multistep electronic health record workflows, and increasingly envision longitudinal care across repeated encounters. This transition expands safety assessment beyond discrete outputs and actions. Through its actions, an agent can help create the clinical state on which its subsequent decisions depend. Consequently, individually defensible actions may compose into an unsafe trajectory, even when no single action is clearly erroneous. We propose recoverability-centered trajectory governance as a clinical synthesis of established safety approaches, linking patient-specific corrective capacity to the continuing justification for delegated authority. Its central objective is clinical recoverability: preserving the opportunity for the human-AI care system to redirect care before clinically acceptable corrective pathways are exhausted. We define recovery margin as the remaining opportunity for such correction, and reauthorization boundaries as conditions requiring delegated authority to end or narrow pending renewed human judgment. This framing distinguishes reversibility, primarily a property of an action, from recoverability, a property of an evolving clinical trajectory. The operational framework combines persistent obligation tracking, independent monitoring, explicit reauthorization, authority contraction, graceful degradation, independent escalation, and verified human takeover. Oversight should concentrate at consequential trajectory junctions. Evaluation should combine trajectory stress testing, component-specific recovery-margin indicators, interruption-and-takeover testing, and population-level surveillance. Trajectory governance complements product lifecycle oversight by examining whether continued patient-specific delegation remains justified as care evolves. Because corrective capacity depends partly on access to timely monitoring and human rescue, recoverability is also an equity issue. The defining safety question is therefore not only whether an action is acceptable but whether continued delegation remains justified. The proposed indicators and governance mechanisms require domain-specific operationalization and empirical validation, including comparison with established safeguards.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is highly prevalent, and noninvasive identification of patients with significant fibrosis remains a clinical challenge. Objective We conducted an exploratory evaluation of explainable machine learning models for predicting significant fibrosis in a US-based cohort of adults with SLD, with particular attention to sensitivity, false-negative risk, and the limitations of using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) alone to assess screening suitability. Methods We evaluated explainable machine learning models for predicting significant fibrosis in a US population–based dataset. A total of 43 routinely available clinical, demographic, anthropometric, laboratory, and lifestyle variables were included. After preprocessing and imputation, data were split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets. The synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) was used to address class imbalance in the training set. Logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, an artificial neural network, and a stacked ensemble were trained and evaluated. Performance metrics included accuracy, precision, recall, F 1 -score, Cohen κ, and the AUROC. Because the intended use case was screening or triage, sensitivity was given particular interpretive importance. In addition to overall discrimination, a primary analytical objective was to examine sensitivity trade-offs, false-negative classifications, and the implications of model performance for screening suitability. Global and local model interpretability were assessed using feature importance, Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values, individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots, and individualized explanations. Results Among 7056 participants, 716 (10.1%) had significant fibrosis. XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination (AUROC 0.79), followed by random forest (AUROC 0.78) and logistic regression (AUROC 0.77); however, XGBoost had low sensitivity (0.17), indicating limited utility for screening at the evaluated threshold. Logistic regression and naive Bayes demonstrated the highest sensitivity (0.65 and 0.55, respectively), suggesting that models with slightly lower discrimination may be more appropriate for triage-oriented use. Across models, waist circumference, BMI, cardiovascular comorbidity, sex, hemoglobin A 1c (HbA 1c ), and liver enzymes were the most influential predictors. Conclusions In this exploratory model development study, moderate discrimination did not necessarily translate into clinically meaningful screening performance. The model with the highest AUROC showed poor sensitivity, indicating a substantial risk of false-negative classifications and limiting its usefulness for screening in its current form. Because imputation was performed before the train-test split, the reported performance estimates may be optimistic and should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of clinical readiness. Leakage-free preprocessing, threshold optimization, calibration assessment, decision curve analysis, external validation, and prospective evaluation are needed before clinical application.

AI-driven skin cancer mobile health apps may help address this need, but their usefulness depends on whether users trust the advice and intend to follow it. Teledermatologist supervision has been proposed to combine AI efficiency with human clinical oversight, but dermatologist shortages make it critical to understand whether such supervision improves patient trust and adherence at the population level, or whether AI-only advice suffices for most users. Objective This study tests whether teledermatologist supervision in an AI-driven skin cancer app affects patient trust and adherence intentions, compared with AI-only advice, and whether these effects differ by motivational context and risk assessment level. Methods The randomized controlled, online vignette experiment with repeated measures was conducted from May to June 2025 as a single-center study among Dutch adults via an academic hospital-based patient panel. Eligible participants were adult members of the Erasmus MC Digital Patient Panel invited by email; those not completing all 4 vignette trials were excluded from the analysis. Participants completed 4 simulated mobile app scenarios varying in advice source (AI-only vs hybrid teledermatologist and AI) and risk assessment level (high vs low). The primary outcomes were trust in the advice (0‐100 scale) and adherence intention (recoded 3-level ordinal scale). Mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data. Results Of the 2707 patient panel members, 879 participated (response rate: 32.5%). Participants were aged 18 to 93 (mean 62.5, SD 12.64) years; 50.4% (n=443) were female, and 21.4% (n=188) had a history of skin cancer. Participants were randomly allocated to motivation conditions (concern: n=438 vs curiosity: n=441). Trust was higher for hybrid advice than AI-only advice (mean 76.9, SE 0.73 vs mean 65.7, SE 0.73; estimated difference 11.98; partial η ²=0.22; P <.001). The odds of adherence were 1.7 times greater with hybrid vs AI-only (odds ratio 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; P <.001). High-risk assessments increased adherence (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8; P <.001), with a moderated effect by motivation ( P =.03), showing stronger adherence with concern vs curiosity. These findings suggest that developers and health care implementers may consider integrating teledermatologist supervision to maximize patient trust of and adherence to advice, potentially improving triaging efficiency and safety.

Conclusions: Parental perspectives highlight both opportunities and challenges for predictive AI integration in neonatal care. AI-based interventions have emerged as scalable approaches to support social connection. A growing body of research has examined the effects of individual AI technologies on improving social connection across diverse devices and care settings. Despite growing evidence of their effects, little attention has been paid to the common pathways through which these interventions support social connection. Objective This scoping review aimed to develop a typology of common categories of support across AI-based interventions and to map how these categories are configured in different intervention contexts. Methods Five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published from 2016 through 2025. Studies were included if they examined AI-based interventions designed to support social connection among older adults, conceptualized as a multidimensional construct encompassing loneliness reduction, social interaction, and behavioral engagement. Results A total of 1110 articles were retrieved, of which 47 met the inclusion criteria. Qualitative and mixed methods studies were the most prevalent (n=32, 68%), with quantitative studies accounting for the remainder (n=15, 32%). Four common support categories were identified: relational interaction (forming ties), emotional support (enhancing interaction quality), functional support (sustaining engagement), and risk detection (reducing constraints). Relational interaction and emotional support were present across all studies. Functional support and risk detection were observed in 70% (n=33) and 17% (n=8) of studies, respectively. The most prevalent configuration combined relational interaction, emotional support, and functional support, forming a companionship-plus-routine pathway that sustained engagement in everyday contexts. Functional support was associated with sustained participation in daily routines and activities, which may have contributed to opportunities for ongoing social interaction. Risk detection, while less prevalent, functioned as a constraint-reducing condition that supported continuity of engagement. Conclusions This review proposes a conceptual framework that shifts attention from specific technologies to the interactional configurations that enable AI to support social connection across care settings. This framework may inform the design and tailoring of AI-based interventions to address the multidimensional nature of social connection among older adults.

The study argues that AI should complement rather than replace expert phonetic interpretation. It concludes that a human-in-the-loop approach integrating computational technologies with linguistic expertise provides the most reliable framework for future research on legal prosody while ensuring methodological transparency, scientific validity, and legal accountability.

record.abstract_text: Humanware represents an emerging paradigm in human cognitive enhancement, extending the AI frontier through integration of human-centered technological interfaces with cognitive learning, metacognition, and adaptive behavioral engagement. Integrating artificial intelligence, machine learning, virtual digital assistance, e-learning, and 5G connectivity, the MQ Mirror exemplifies an interactive neurocognitive interface designed to place humans at the centre of technological engagement instead of the device. MQ Mirrors multimodal capabilities comprise personalized coaching, instructional guidance, physical fitness, auditory stimulation, motivational reinforcement, and spiritually oriented reflection. Such an interface supports cognitive engagement, verbal reasoning, spatial processing, attentional regulation, digital literacy, and metacognitive awareness particularly in young adults. On the other hand, technology-centric gadgets or devices risk promoting addictive design, over-dependency, psychological withdrawals, sleep deprivation, disrupted socialization, sedentary lifestyles with ripple effects of anxiety and depression especially in adolescents. This case-study depicts how independent active learning, cognitive autonomy, holistic wellness and individual development across intellectual, physical, and psychosocial domains is orchestrated through Humanware. This original research proposes that Mirrored Intelligence could establish complementary neural networks facilitating human cognitive enhancement with significant implications for cognitive neuroscience, neuropsychology, and educational technology in future.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence has rapidly entered higher education teaching. A growing body of empirical research examines faculty attitudes and intention to adopt tools such as ChatGPT. However, emerging evidence suggests that intention does not consistently translate into sustained pedagogical integration. Unlike previous syntheses of AI in higher education, which have focused on applications, perceptions, or acceptance, this study addresses this discrepancy through a systematic review of empirical research published between 2023 and 2026. Following the PRISMA protocol, the review identified 150 methodologically adequate studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science. A focused explanatory synthesis was conducted on 33 core investigations that included both intention-related constructs and indicators of pedagogical use. The analysis mapped publication trends, research designs, theoretical orientations, and predictors of behavioral intention, and examined mechanisms underlying the intention–practice gap. The findings indicate that technology acceptance models dominate the literature and consistently explain intention formation through perceived usefulness, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence. Nevertheless, only one-third of the core studies explicitly identified a discrepancy between intention and enacted pedagogical practice, whereas the majority did not directly examine or report this relationship. The evidence suggests that pedagogical capability, particularly TPACK-related competence and instructional design knowledge, mediates the translation of intention into structured classroom integration. Institutional support, governance clarity, professional development, and identity-related factors moderate the strength of this process. The review proposes a conditional intention–practice translation model integrating UTAUT and TPACK. The findings suggest that the central challenge in higher education lies not in faculty willingness, but in developing pedagogical capability within supportive institutional environments that enable sustained instructional transformation.

record.abstract_text: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education in Pakistan has created both opportunities and concerns for educators, researchers, and policymakers. ChatGPT, a generative AI tool developed by OpenAI, can support teaching, learning, assessment, research, and academic work. This study examined how experienced academicians view its benefits, limitations, and ethical implications in Pakistani higher education. A qualitative exploratory design was used in this study. Twelve experienced academicians from different higher education institutions in Pakistan were selected purposively and interviewed through a semi-structured guide. The interviews were transcribed and analysed through familiarization, coding, development and review of themes. ChatGPT was used only to help organize provisional codes; the researchers checked its suggestions against the transcripts and made the final analytical decisions. Five themes were identified: teaching, learning, assessment, research, and ethics. Participants reported that ChatGPT supported lesson planning, content preparation, student engagement, idea generation, academic writing, and research productivity. They also noted that it enables students to understand difficult topics, improve their writing skills, and obtain immediate academic support. Main concerns were identified as plagiarism, over-reliance on AI-generated content, weaker critical thinking, and the absence of clear institutional policies. The findings show that ChatGPT may be useful in higher education when its use is guided by academic judgment and clear rules. Universities should redesign assessment, prepare ethical guidelines, train faculty, and strengthen AI literacy. The study offers practical information for teachers, administrators, and policymakers planning the responsible use of generative AI in Pakistan.

record.abstract_text: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic process automation (RPA) is transforming the technological environment in which legal relations arise and are implemented. Unlike traditional automation based primarily on predetermined rules, AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, identify patterns, generate predictions, adapt their behaviour and select among alternative outputs. This creates new challenges concerning legal attribution, liability, contractual relations and intellectual property. The article examines the relationship between AI and RPA from legal, technological and inter- disciplinary perspectives, with particular attention to the relationship between technological auton- omy and legal personality. It argues that technological autonomy cannot, by itself, constitute grounds for granting an AI system legal personality, since legal personality is a normative construct estab- lished by law. The relevant question is whether a special legal status would provide an effective response to specific regulatory problems. The study distinguishes conventional automated information systems, AI systems that assist human decision-making, and highly autonomous AI systems. While traditional legal mechanisms may generally be sufficient for conventional automation, AI-assisted and highly autonomous sys- tems require additional safeguards concerning transparency, traceability, human oversight and accountability. The article also examines the informational structure of AI and the need to distin- guish hardware, software, algorithms, models and data in relation to property rights, intellectual property and liability. The concept of electronic personality is analysed in the context of the contemporary European approach, particularly Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), which establishes a risk-based framework focused on safety, fundamental rights, transparency and human oversight. For Ukraine, the article proposes a gradual regulatory model based on coherent terminology, risk- based classification, transparency, traceability, human oversight and clear liability rules. Further regulation should address automated contractual activity, AI-generated results and risk insurance. A special electronic legal status should be considered only after sufficient technological, legislative and judicial practice has demonstrated that existing legal mechanisms are inadequate.

record.abstract_text: The contemporary literary landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by the rise of Instapoetry: short, visual, and emotionally direct verse disseminated primarily through Instagram, a platform whose image-first architecture and recommender systems privilege affectively engaging content. This article argues that the dominance of this poetic form represents not a superficial cultural trend but an adaptive response to a digitally mediated attention economy. It advances an integrative theoretical framework explaining Instapoetry through the convergence of three dimensions: algorithmic, psychological, and cultural. First, algorithmic amplification on Instagram leverages patterns of repetition and social proof to promote specific formal styles. Second, the cognitive state of the platform’s users—marked by social media fatigue and elevated cognitive load—produces a preference for content high in processing fluency. Third, the cultural motifs that dominate Instapoetry function as accessible affective schemas, enabling readers to engage in self-expression, identity construction, and emotional validation. Drawing on research in media studies, cognitive science, and feminist literary criticism—and referencing the influential work of early Instapoets such as Rupi Kaur and Amanda Lovelace—this paper proposes a multidisciplinary account of how digital infrastructures and human psychology jointly shape contemporary poetic production and reception.

record.title: Artificial intelligence for poultry disease and health monitoring: a narrative review of computer vision, multimodal sensing, edge AI, and generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Poultry diseases and welfare issues can lead to significant production losses, compromise food safety, and create a need for ongoing farm monitoring. This narrative review summarises 81 peer-reviewed research papers published between 2016 and 2026 focusing on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for monitoring poultry diseases and health. The papers were grouped into the following categories, namely disease diagnosis, health and welfare monitoring, mortality and biosecurity surveillance, and post-harvest food safety, and are summarised in a study-level appendix by modality, technique and reported data details. Conventional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, YOLO-based object detection, transformer models, explainable AI, multimodal fusion, IoT, edge AI, federated learning, generative AI, and vision-language models are the focus of the reviewed literature. The most common methods are image and faecal-image analysis, complemented by audio, thermal, video, behavioural, and environmental sensing. The trend in recent work is to use lightweight models on local devices and to integrate multiple modalities. Some limitations to direct comparison of reported results include small sample sizes and the nature of the datasets in some studies, differences in class definitions, unbalanced classes, inconsistent validation protocols, and limited cross-farm testing. Cross-farm generalisation, standardised benchmarking, explainability, prospective veterinary validation, privacy-preserving collaboration features, and cost-effective edge deployment are highlighted as key priorities. Future work should involve creating multi-country and multi-breed benchmark datasets, developing commercially validated decision-support tools and poultry-specific foundation models, and implementing continual-learning systems and multimodal fusion frameworks. The review suggests that AI has the potential to enhance precision poultry production, but successful long-term implementation of AI in the field requires not only high accuracy but also robustness, interpretability, and affordability.

record.abstract_text: Debates concerning generative artificial intelligence increasingly address not only what these systems can produce, but also who receives credit, who is compensated, and whose professional authority is safeguarded. This study examines how news and industry publications in the United States and Mexico represented AI and creative labor between 2023 and 2026. It draws on a comparative, cross-sectional quantitative content analysis of a purposively stratified corpus of 120 articles, focusing on represented harms, worker agency, institutional responsibility, proposed responses, and dominant frames. Coverage in both countries addressed displacement, compensation, authorship, and unauthorized reproduction, but differed in how it interpreted these concerns. Labor rights and collective action constituted the dominant frame in 50.0% of United States articles and 6.7% of Mexican articles, whereas legal and intellectual property concerns predominated in 50.0% of Mexican articles and 8.3% of United States articles. Regulation or legislation appeared in 86.7% of Mexican coverage and 36.7% of United States coverage, while collective bargaining or labor action appeared more frequently in the United States sample. The regulatory contrast remained evident across analyses restricted by publication period and publication category. From a Media Ecology perspective, these patterns suggest that coverage helps define which harms, actors, and remedies become publicly visible. The study therefore identifies differences in the institutional meaning assigned to AI-related disruption without making claims about audience-level effects.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Drug prescription review is a key link in ensuring patient medication safety and improving the quality of medicine. The traditional manual review model is limited by human resources, the speed of information updates and individual experience differences, making it difficult to cope with the increasingly complex environment of medication review. This article is a narrative review of the development history, core technical architecture, main application models, implementation benefits, and the challenges and future trends of information-based drug prescription review. Rule engines, clinical decision support, machine learning and generative artificial intelligence have extended review from static rule checking towards risk prediction and text understanding, but these technologies differ substantially in validation, interpretability and maturity. Information-based review achieves real-time, standardised interception and alerting of prescription risks at scale and reduces the rate at which recognised prescribing errors reach the patient; the evidence for reductions in preventable adverse drug events and in patient outcomes such as admissions and mortality is, however, weaker, heterogeneous and dominated by single-centre or before-and-after designs. System limitations, clinical adaptability, data quality, alert fatigue, interoperability, equity and law still require attention, and future value will depend less on algorithmic sophistication than on validation in real settings, interoperable data and human oversight.

record.abstract_text: This study examines prompt literacy among future computer science teachers in the context of solving and debugging programming tasks with ChatGPT. It focuses on students' perceptions of prompt literacy, their understanding of responsible AI use, documented practices of verifying and modifying AI-assisted solutions, and patterns of academic performance. A descriptive multi-method study was conducted during a 16-week programming course involving 113 future computer science teachers at Kh. Dosmukhamedov Atyrau University, Kazakhstan. Data were collected through questionnaires, student programming submissions, ChatGPT-use disclosure notes, reflective comments, code-similarity screening, and course-grade records. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative content analysis was used to identify recurring patterns in students' reported use, verification, and revision of AI-generated solutions. The findings were compared across data sources to address the research questions without testing causal effects or participant-level associations. The 20-item Prompt-Literacy Perceptions Questionnaire demonstrated high overall internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.94). Students generally reported positive perceptions of ChatGPT for code generation, debugging, and explaining programming logic. They also recognized the importance of verifying AI-generated outputs and disclosing substantial AI assistance. However, students' documentation of verification and modification practices was frequently general rather than detailed. Pairwise code-similarity screening identified relatively few submission pairs exceeding the predefined 50% similarity threshold. Mean academic scores were numerically close across practical assignments and independent control tasks, although differences in assessment conditions and grading criteria limited direct comparisons. The findings highlight the importance of integrating prompt literacy, critical verification, and transparent documentation of AI use into computer science teacher education. Positive perceptions of responsible ChatGPT use did not necessarily correspond to detailed documentation of verification and revision practices. Code-similarity results cannot independently establish whether students modified AI-generated solutions. Furthermore, the descriptive single-cohort design does not support conclusions about causal effects or improvements in prompt-literacy competence. The study emphasizes the pedagogical value of making students' reasoning, verification, and responsible AI-use practices explicit during programming instruction.

record.abstract_text: Introduction This study aims to analyse university students' perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in their academic education, exploring how they construct meaning around its use and how these representations influence notions of learning, authorship and critical literacy in higher education. Methods The sample comprised 20 students from Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru. The Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET) was employed as a qualitative elicitation approach using images and metaphorical narratives, applied via a two-phase protocol: a) a pre-task involving the independent selection of seven images; and b) a guided elicitation phase, based on questions that explore the participant's perception through analogies, sensory contrasts and emotional narratives. Results Within this corpus, participants articulated ambivalent representations of GenAI through several distinct metaphorical configurations, including an “other” to which participants attribute agency (a silent companion or tutor) and a pragmatic cognitive extension valued for its efficiency. These representations highlight a reconfiguration of the relationship between students and processes of knowledge production, blurring traditional boundaries between technological assistance, collaboration and authorship. On an emotional level, some accounts represented GenAI as an emotional buffer, offering relief from academic overload; however, this relief coexists with ethical vigilance and unease about “crossing a line” in academic honesty, reflecting processes of negotiation over intellectual responsibility and the legitimate use of generative systems in educational contexts. Discussion Regarding institutional adaptation, metaphors of misalignment and accounts of GenAI bridging gaps in academic support point to perceived gaps in institutional guidance and to the importance of pedagogical mediation, including clearer approaches to teaching and assessment in a context where GenAI is already part of university life. Taken together, the accounts show how participants interpret GenAI as a context-specific form of academic support and guidance. These representations link the negotiation of trust and authorship to the perceived accessibility of university support, offering insights into critical literacy and institutional mediation.

This qualitative study explored the experiences and perceptions of first-year students ( n = 10) using AI-generated reflective visuals (AIGRVs) as part of a reflective assessment approach in a general education course at a Middle Eastern university. Basic quantitative results from the same surveys, including responses to Likert-scale statements, were also analysed and used as supplementary evidence to support the qualitative findings. record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can transform teaching, learning, assessment and research in higher education. In Ecuador, the adoption of ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models is driving academic interest, yet little is known about the scientific production that addresses it. This systematic mapping review, reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, maps the scientific production on generative artificial intelligence that explicitly refers to Ecuador, indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2024 and 2026, in order to establish the weight that higher education holds within it. No disciplinary filter was applied to the query, so that this weight could be measured rather than assumed. The search, executed on 4 July 2026, retrieved 57 records (all 16 Web of Science records were also in Scopus, so the corpus comes in practice from Scopus; regional databases were not searched); after removing 16 duplicates and excluding 9 records, 32 documents were mapped with bibliometric indicators (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer), and the 18 higher education studies with primary data were subjected to a focused synthesis that included the appraisal of their methodological quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Higher education accounts for 20 of the 32 documents (63%); the other 12 are spread over political communication and journalism, legal and technical applications and four smaller domains. A sensitivity search with synonyms, Spanish terms and the year 2023, run on 15 October 2026, gave a similar share (44 of 73 documents, 60%). Within the higher education corpus, perceptions and acceptance of GAI are the most frequent outcome domain (16 of 18 studies); learning outcomes appear in six, but only two measure them directly. Eight studies use descriptive or cross-sectional designs, and none is randomised or longitudinal. ChatGPT is the most frequently examined tool (11 of 18). Sample representativeness and control of confounding were the most frequent methodological weaknesses. The findings highlight the need for experimental and longitudinal research evaluating the impact of GAI on Ecuadorian higher education.

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being rapidly adopted in education, prompting growing interest in its application to Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). This scoping review examines studies in which a generative system acts as a pedagogical agent that directly mediates learning about sustainability. Following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported under PRISMA-ScR, searches in Scopus, Web of Science and ERIC retrieved 172 records, of which 25 studies, reported in 26 publications and published between 2024 and 2026, met the eligibility criteria. Charting combined descriptive variables with reviewer-assigned interpretive codes governed by explicit decision rules. The corpus is close to evenly distributed between Global North and Global South settings, concentrated in higher education, and pedagogically well embedded: 20 of the 21 implemented interventions are integrated into instruction rather than running alongside it, although only 11 frame the generative activity with briefing, debriefing or guided reflection. Generative systems are deployed most frequently as dialogic tutors and instructional co-designers, and all studies target cognitive outcomes, although measured change in learners is evidenced in ten and against a comparison condition in only five. The review also identifies where the field can consolidate: explicit operationalisation of sustainability competency frameworks, designs able to isolate the generative component, delayed measurement of outcomes, deliberative configurations that keep normative judgement with the learner, and attention to the environmental footprint of the tools themselves. Four evidence-informed design principles are proposed to guide this consolidation.

record.abstract_text: Background Emergency medicine is characterized by urgency, criticality, severity, and diversity, which places high demands on undergraduate medical education. Traditional lecture-based teaching has limitations in developing students' advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer ability. Although virtual simulation and case-based learning (CBL) have demonstrated benefits in medical education, their combined application in emergency medicine teaching has not been systematically evaluated, especially based on artificial intelligence (AI). This study primarily aimed to investigate whether the integrated AI-powered virtual simulation combined with CBL could improve students' higher-order clinical competencies and clinical transfer ability, and secondarily to obtain empirical evidence to support the optimization of undergraduate emergency medicine teaching. Methods Third-year undergraduate students majoring in clinical medicine were selected as the research subjects and randomly divided into the control group and the experimental group. The control group adopted the traditional teaching method, while the experimental group adopted the AI-enabled virtual simulation combined with real emergency case teaching method. The learning situation of the virtual simulation platform was automatically recorded by the platform, and the teaching effect was evaluated through theoretical scores, objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) scores, clinical practice tracking evaluation (including advanced clinical ability and clinical transfer effect evaluation), comprehensive evaluation of learning psychology, and teaching satisfaction questionnaire. record.abstract_text: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate human-like text, it is becoming an increasingly pressing empirical and societal question: how can AI-generated text be distinguished from human-written text? record.abstract_text: With AI’s increasing role in digital marketing, a brand’s transparency about its use of AI could act as an informational signal of accountability. However, the interpretation consumers make of such transparency might vary with their knowledge of AI and their perception of persuasive intent. This study examines the relationship between perceived AI marketing transparency, brand trust, and purchase intention and the role of perceived manipulative intent as a mechanism and AI literacy as a boundary condition. We surveyed 387 matched Pakistani consumers, in two waves. AI literacy was operationalised with the core 18-item AI literacy dimensions of the MAILS instrument (use and apply AI, know and understand AI, detect AI, and AI ethics), whereas the remaining MAILS dimensions were treated as separate constructs. We tested the hypotheses using regression-based simple mediation (PROCESS Model 4) and first-stage moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 7). Perceived AI marketing transparency was positively associated with brand trust (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). Brand trust carried a significant indirect association between perceived AI marketing transparency and purchase intention (indirect effect = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.11]); the direct association was not statistically significant (c′ = 0.10, p = 0.081). Perceived manipulative intent was negatively associated with brand trust (b = −0.25, p < 0.001). AI literacy positively moderated the association between perceived AI marketing transparency and perceived manipulative intent (B = 0.13, p = 0.031), such that this association was positive and significant only at high AI literacy (B = 0.25, p < 0.001). The conditional indirect association was statistically distinguishable from zero only at high AI literacy (effect = −0.06, 95% CI [−0.13, −0.01]). The index of moderated mediation was statistically significant at the 5% level (index = −0.03, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.001]) but the CI was close to the null value. The results are consistent with both theoretically opposite mechanisms suggested: an accountability-related association between perceived transparency and brand trust, and a conditional suspicion-related indirect association via perceived manipulative intent, which were analysed under the umbrella of two different empirical models. The interaction was small and the moderated-mediation evidence was statistically weak and should be considered a preliminary rather than a general finding of the negative effects on transparency. One of the contributions of the study is distinguishing perceived transparency from its interpretation, and examining core AI literacy competencies in addition to a focused measure of persuasion knowledge activation in the context of AI marketing and signaling research. Finally, practical implications highlight the importance of AI disclosure being credible and context-specific, not necessarily a strategy that builds trust.

record.title: Does Generative AI Reduce Mental Effort at The Expense of Deep Thinking? An Experimental Investigation of Cognitive Load and Knowledge Retention
record.venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development

record.abstract_text: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.

record.title: Capability atrophy: When AI automation erodes the dynamic capabilities it was meant to build

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Firms adopt artificial intelligence (AI) automation to strengthen their dynamic capabilities, yet automation can also remove managers from the routines through which those capabilities are renewed. Drawing on the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities, organizational learning theory, and the automation–augmentation paradox, this conceptual paper develops the concept of capability atrophy and specifies when AI automation weakens, rather than builds, firm-level dynamic capabilities. Theory synthesis across research on skill erosion, organizational learning, and human–AI collaboration yields nine propositions, together with a multilevel, multi-wave mixed-methods design that uses behavioral and system-discontinuance measures to test them. The propositions hold that automation intensity relates to dynamic capability change in an inverted-U pattern, turning negative beyond a substitution threshold. Erosion travels through reduced experiential engagement, weaker skill retention, and poorer reliance calibration, and it becomes organizational when tacit knowledge is concentrated and apprenticeship paths close. Retained decision roles, frequent exceptions, and task variety are proposed to raise the threshold, whereas analytics capability alone is not. The paper places capability atrophy within existing skill-erosion research and adds a firm-level, conditional account with explicit falsification criteria. For practice, it implies that managers should track override rates, unaided diagnosis time, and other observable indicators of capability retention alongside the returns on AI investment.
